Why the nozzle matters

A pick error is a nozzle decision, not a machine decision

Two boards from the same feeder, the same program, the same head - and one skips 0402s while the other runs clean. The variable is almost always the tip: the wrong bore for the component width, a worn edge, or a nozzle that was never meant for the part. Getting the nozzle right is cheaper than buying a new machine.

01

The right bore, or the part skews

Every standard JUKI nozzle is published against an applicable component width. A tip too wide loses the vacuum seal on a small chip; a tip too narrow cannot seat a large body. Matching the bore to the part is the first cause of a clean pick.

02

Wear is a downtime line, not a consumable line

A worn tip raises the mis-pick rate long before anyone logs it as a fault. The mounter retries, the head waits, and the operator clears a jam that the catalogue would have predicted. Nozzle life is a throughput number wearing a spare-parts label.

03

Odd-form parts need a different tool, not a smaller chip

Connectors, transformers and polarised parts do not sit on a flat vacuum tip. Slot, gripper and pipe nozzles exist for exactly these parts, and choosing the type is a design decision made before the line runs, not a fix applied after it stops.

How to match a nozzle

From component drawing to a nozzle that runs

Selecting a pickup nozzle is a short, repeatable sequence: measure the part, pick the tip family, size the bore to the component width, then confirm the shaft, the material and the pick test. Southern Machinery runs this sequence against your actual component, not a catalogue photograph.

01

Measure the component

Record the body width, length, height and weight. The width drives the bore; the weight drives the vacuum.

02

Pick the tip family

Flat chips take a vacuum tip. Leads and slots take a slot nozzle; bulky or polarised parts take a gripper or a pipe nozzle.

03

Size the bore to the width

The catalogue maps each standard nozzle to an applicable component width, so the bore is chosen from a published band, not by eye.

04

Match the shaft and slider

The nozzle must seat on the correct JUKI head and, where used, the standard Automatic Tool Changer shaft.

05

Choose material and tip

Standard bodies are a copper alloy; fine-pitch tips use polyurethane cups; pipe nozzles use interchangeable rubber tips.

06

Machine the tip geometry

Outer and inner diameter, chamfer and slot width are cut to the drawing so the seal forms on the first pick.

07

Test the pick rate

The nozzle is proven on the part before it ships; Southern Machinery quotes a 99.99 percent pickup rate on its own decks.

08

Install and teach

Fit to the head, set the pickup height and vacuum, then confirm the pick window on the machine.

09

Log and rotate

Track the mis-pick rate per nozzle and replace on trend, before the wear becomes a line stop.

The steps below describe the selection method Southern Machinery applies. Tip dimensions and machine fit are quoted from the JUKI application catalogue; the final configuration is confirmed against your component and head.

Insights

Eight notes on the last millimetre of the pick

Long-form notes on SMT pickup nozzles, written for process engineers and buyers who have to keep a JUKI line running, not just order a spare.

ARTICLE 01Your Mis-pick Rate Is a Nozzle Problem Before It Is a Machine Problem

Before you call the machine vendor, look at the tip in the head.

Full articles are in English. The summary above carries the argument in your language.

A line is throwing one 0402 in three hundred. The program is clean, the feeder is new, the head has been serviced, and the machine vendor is about to be asked for a visit. Before anyone books that visit, take the nozzle out of the head and look at the tip.

The reason is that the pick is the only part of the placement cycle that touches the component, and it is the step with the most ways to fail quietly. A bore a fraction too wide for the part loses the vacuum seal on one side. A tip with a worn edge seals inconsistently. A nozzle chosen for a part that has since changed keeps 'working' while the mis-pick rate creeps up, because nobody declared a fault - the machine just retries and the throughput drops.

Work the failure from the tip outward. First, confirm the nozzle type against the component width band the catalogue publishes - if the part has moved size, the bore may simply be wrong now. Second, inspect the tip edge under magnification for a chip or a rounded chamfer. Third, check the vacuum level and the pickup height, because a low seal often looks like a bad nozzle. Only after those three do you call the machine vendor.

That sequence is how Southern Machinery matches a nozzle in the first place: measure the part, pick the tip family, size the bore to the published width band, then set the seal. The standard 500-series tips run from 0.7 mm to 9.5 mm outer bore, each mapped to a component width, so the right bore is a lookup rather than a guess - and when no standard tip fits, the same method produces a custom one.

The habit that pays is a monthly tip inspection on the highest-mis-pick head, logged against the nozzle part number. A wear trend you can see is a stop you can schedule; a wear trend you cannot see is the surprise that eats a shift.

Pull the nozzle from your worst head today, photograph the tip, and check the part width against the bore you are running. If they disagree, you have found the problem; if they agree, you have a clean starting point for the next step - and a photograph worth sending to your nozzle supplier.

ARTICLE 02How to Read a Nozzle Bore Table Without Guessing

Outer bore, inner bore and applicable width do three different jobs.

Full articles are in English. The summary above carries the argument in your language.

A nozzle table has three columns that look like they say the same thing and do not: outer bore, inner bore, and applicable component width. Reading them correctly is the difference between a tip that seals and a tip that skews the part.

The confusion costs real money. A buyer who matches only the outer bore will pick a tip that physically covers the part but cannot hold it, because the vacuum is applied through the inner bore. A buyer who ignores the applicable width will seat a part that is outside the tip's designed band, and the pick will be marginal - good on a clean sample, bad on a full reel.

Read the three columns as a job each one does. Outer bore is the contact diameter that has to sit on the part. Inner bore is the vacuum opening that has to be small enough to seal against the part body. Applicable width is the catalogue's own answer to the question 'what part is this tip for' - it already accounts for the first two, so it is the column to select from when you have a component drawing.

The JUKI catalogue publishes all three for the standard families. Nozzle 503 is 1.0 mm outer and 0.6 mm inner and is mapped to components 0.75 to 1.45 mm wide; nozzle 506 is 5.0 mm outer and 3.2 mm inner for 4.0 to 7.0 mm. When you specify from the width band first and confirm the bores second, you are using the table the way it was written.

Over time, the applicable-width column is the one to keep current. Component sizes drift when a supplier changes a part, and a nozzle that was correct last quarter can be one band off this quarter without anyone changing a thing on the head.

Take one part you place daily, find its width, and look up the catalogue band it falls in. Then check what nozzle is actually in the head today. If they do not match, that is your first easy correction.

ARTICLE 03When to Stop Using a Vacuum Tip and Start Using a Gripper

Three signs the part is telling you it needs a mechanical grip.

Full articles are in English. The summary above carries the argument in your language.

Vacuum is the default, and for flat chips it is the right answer. But there is a moment on every odd-form line when the vacuum tip stops being the tool and starts being the problem, and the part tells you so in three ways.

The first sign is a part that will not seat flat, so the vacuum never gets a clean seal - a connector with a moulded body, a transformer with a bobbin, a polarised capacitor with a curved face. The second is a part that tips over on pickup because its centre of mass is above the bore. The third is a part that gets crushed or skewed because the only thing holding it is suction on a small area.

The decision is mechanical, not a bigger vacuum. If the part has leads you can straddle, a slot nozzle grips the body between the slot walls. If the part is bulky or polarised and you need to clamp it, a gripper nozzle holds it across a published 0.8 to 5.2 mm range. If the part is a large body, a socket or a shield that you must lift without a seal, a pipe nozzle with a rubber tip carries it.

Southern Machinery manufactures all three families for the JUKI 700 and 2000 groups, and the slot width, arm height and rubber-tip options are published per type, so the choice is a lookup against the part geometry rather than an experiment on the line. When none of the standard slot, gripper or pipe tips fits, the same shop machines a custom one.

The recurring review is to list the parts that still cause retries and ask, for each, whether it is actually a vacuum part at all. A surprising number of chronic mis-picks are not nozzle wear - they are a vacuum tip asked to do a gripper's job.

Pick your three most troublesome odd-form parts and, for each, decide whether the fix is a slot, a gripper or a pipe nozzle. Send the three parts and you will get three tip recommendations, or a straight answer that one of them needs a custom tool.

ARTICLE 04The Two 500-Series Revisions and Why Backward Fit Is Not Assumed

Same nozzle number, different part number, different machine.

Full articles are in English. The summary above carries the argument in your language.

The same nozzle number can be two different parts. On the JUKI 500 series that distinction decides whether the nozzle fits your machine at all, and it is the single most common order mistake on older mounters.

The trap is that the type number - 500, 501, 502 and so on - is printed on both revisions. A buyer orders 'nozzle 503', receives a part, and finds it will not seat correctly on a KE-2020, because the part they received is the new revision, which is built for KE-2050, KE-2060 and FX-1 and is explicitly not compatible with the earlier KE-2010 to 2040.

The fix is to specify by part number, not type number. The catalogue carries two columns for the 500 series: the original E36xx7290A0 family and the new 40011046 / 40001339 series. The compatibility matrix in the catalogue marks the original as fitting the whole KE-2010 to 2060 and FX-1 range, and the new revision as fitting only KE-2050, 2060 and FX-1. Read the matrix for your exact model before you order.

Southern Machinery quotes against both revisions and will confirm which one your head takes, because the type number alone is not enough to place the order correctly. This is also why the compatibility point is carried in the Open points section of this page rather than buried in a footnote - it is where the mistakes happen.

As your fleet ages, the revision question gets more important, not less. A mixed line of older and newer heads means two nozzle stocks under one type number, and the cost of getting it wrong is a machine that sits idle while the right revision is couriered in.

Write your machine's exact model and firmware on the enquiry, and ask for the part number to be confirmed against it. If a supplier quotes you by type number alone, send this back to them.

ARTICLE 05Nozzle Wear Is a Throughput Number Wearing a Spare-Parts Label

What a rising mis-pick trend costs you before anyone logs a fault.

Full articles are in English. The summary above carries the argument in your language.

Nobody budgets for nozzle wear, because it never fails as an event. It fails as a trend - a mis-pick rate that climbs by a fraction of a percent a week until one day the line is slow and nobody can say when it started.

The consequence is that the cost hides in throughput, not in spares. A worn tip does not stop the machine; it makes the machine retry. Each retry is a fraction of a second, and a few fractions of a second across thousands of picks a shift is a percentage of your line rate that you have already sold to the customer as delivered capacity. By the time anyone replaces the nozzle, you have run weeks at a rate you are not being paid for.

The way to see it is to log the mis-pick rate per head against the nozzle part number, weekly, and set a replacement trend rather than a replacement schedule. A schedule changes nozzles too often or too late; a trend changes them when the data says the tip is drifting. The trigger is the slope, not the absolute number.

This is where a nozzle with a longer, more consistent life earns its price. Southern Machinery's own decks quote a service life of more than 24 months and a 99.99 percent pickup rate; treat those as targets to verify on your part, but the point stands - a tip that holds its geometry longer flattens the wear curve and delays the drift into lost throughput.

The habit that closes the loop is a monthly review of the mis-pick trend against the nozzle change log. When a head's rate drops after a change, you have proof of the wear cost; when it does not, you have learned the problem was never the nozzle.

Start logging mis-pick rate per head this month, by nozzle part number. You will not fix a problem you cannot see, and this is the cheapest line-rate number you can collect.

ARTICLE 06Selecting a Nozzle for Odd-Form Parts: Slot, Gripper or Pipe

A short decision order that keeps the wrong tool off the head.

Full articles are in English. The summary above carries the argument in your language.

Odd-form nozzle selection looks like guesswork until you realise it is a fixed order of questions. Answer them in sequence and the right tip - slot, gripper or pipe - falls out almost on its own.

The reason people get it wrong is that they start from the machine. They look at what the head can hold and pick the closest vacuum tip, then debug the pick afterwards. The part does not care what the head can hold; it cares how it can be carried without skewing, tipping or being crushed.

Start from the part, in this order. One: can a vacuum seal form on a flat face of the part? If yes, stay on a vacuum tip. Two: does the part have leads you can straddle and a body the slot walls can grip? If yes, it is a slot nozzle. Three: is the part bulky or polarised and does it need to be clamped rather than sealed? If yes, it is a gripper, and you check the gripping range against the body. Four: is it a large body, a socket or a shield that must be lifted without a reliable seal? If yes, it is a pipe nozzle with a rubber tip to protect the part.

The catalogue supports this order with published numbers. Slot nozzles carry a slot width and length per type; gripper nozzles carry an arm width and height across a 0.8 to 5.2 mm gripping range; pipe nozzles carry outer and inner bores with interchangeable rubber tips - all listed for both the 700 and 2000 machine families, so once you know the answer you know the part.

The recurring value of using the same order is that new engineers make the same choice as the experienced ones. A decision sequence written down is a standard; a rule of thumb in someone's head is a risk when they leave.

Take one odd-form part you are fighting today and run it through the four questions in order. Whatever tip the sequence points to, send the part and the answer and ask for that configuration to be confirmed.

ARTICLE 07The Pick-Test You Should Insist On Before a Nozzle Ships

Which numbers to ask for, and which marketing figure to treat as a target.

Full articles are in English. The summary above carries the argument in your language.

A nozzle supplier can put a number on a datasheet and a number on a marketing deck, and the two are not the same kind of promise. Knowing which figure to insist on before you buy is most of what separates a good nozzle order from an expensive sample.

The problem is that the headline number - a pickup rate, a life in months - is usually the best case on a clean part, not the guaranteed case on yours. A 99.99 percent pickup rate measured on a standard 0603 tells you the shop can make a good tip; it does not tell you the tip will hold that rate on your moulded connector with its flash and its tolerance stack.

So ask for four things, in this order. One: the pick test on your actual part, not a catalogue part - a count of picks and mis-picks on a sample run. Two: the tip geometry drawing you are being quoted against, so the bore matches the component width band. Three: the material and tip construction as stated, not as implied. Four: the part number revision for your exact machine model.

On a JUKI nozzle from Southern Machinery, the first two are the ones that matter most. The deck's 99.99 percent and 24-month figures are the manufacturer's own claims and should be read as targets; the copper-alloy body and the published bore table are catalogue facts; and the pick test on your part is the only number that predicts your line. Ask for the test, and treat the marketing figure as the starting assumption it is.

The discipline that keeps this honest over time is to write down, for every nozzle you approve, which numbers were verified on your part and which were taken from a datasheet. Six months later, when a nozzle underperforms, that record tells you whether you were sold a promise or given a measurement.

On your next nozzle enquiry, ask for a pick test on your own part and the drawing the bore is quoted against. If the supplier can give you both, the marketing number stops mattering - and you have a real basis to approve or reject.

ARTICLE 08Building a Nozzle Spares Kit That Matches Your Real Part Mix

How to stock the tips you actually run, not the ones on the datasheet.

Full articles are in English. The summary above carries the argument in your language.

Most nozzle spares kits are built from a datasheet and then discovered, under pressure, to be missing the one tip that the line actually runs. The fix is to stock against your real part mix, not against the catalogue's completeness.

The reason is that a datasheet lists every nozzle the machine supports, but your line only ever places a fraction of them. A kit that mirrors the datasheet is large, expensive and still wrong, because it is optimised for coverage rather than for the parts you place every shift. When a tip wears at 2 a.m., the part you need is the one you did not stock.

Build the kit from your placement history. Pull the last quarter of board programs, count the distinct component widths you actually place, and map each to the catalogue nozzle band it falls in. The set of nozzles those bands point to is your core stock - usually far smaller than the datasheet and exactly matched to what runs.

Then add the odd-form layer separately. The vacuum tips cover the chips, but your connectors, transformers and polarised parts need slot, gripper and pipe nozzles, and those are the tips most often missing from a chip-focused kit. Southern Machinery's catalogue covers all of these families for the JUKI 700 and 2000 groups, and machines custom tips where a standard one does not fit, so the odd-form layer can be specified from the same part list.

The review that keeps the kit right is quarterly, against the same placement history. New parts enter the mix, old ones leave, and a kit that is refreshed against real data every quarter never carries the dead stock of a datasheet mirror.

Pull your last quarter of board programs, extract the distinct component widths, and map them to nozzle bands. That list is your spares kit - and it is almost certainly different from the one you have on the shelf.

FAQ

Questions buyers ask before the first sample

Which JUKI machines do these nozzles fit?
The JUKI application catalogue maps the 500 series to the KE-2010, 2020, 2030, 2040, 2050, 2060 and FX-1 heads, and the 1xx and 2xx families to the 700 series. Southern Machinery also lists a RES-1 serial family. Confirm your exact head and firmware before ordering.
What tip sizes are available?
Standard tip outer bores run from 0.7 mm (nozzle 501/502) to 9.5 mm (508 and 106), with inner bores from 0.2 mm to 8.0 mm. Each catalogue nozzle is published against an applicable component width, so the bore is chosen from a band rather than by eye.
What are the nozzles made of?
The catalogue states a copper-alloy body and tip, with polyurethane cups on fine-pitch tips and interchangeable rubber tips on pipe nozzles. No tungsten-carbide or ceramic claim is made for these JUKI rows in the supplied documents; the Southern Machinery supplier catalogue tags the JUKI rows as METAL / PAD.
Can you make a custom nozzle?
Yes. Southern Machinery describes itself as specialized in the design and manufacture of SMT nozzles and lists a custom nozzle family, including slot, gripper and pipe types and a JUKI CN-SM-2713 custom part. Custom nozzles are built to the standard slider shaft and the standard Automatic Tool Changer.
Is the 500-series part number interchangeable with my older machine?
Not always. The catalogue lists two revisions: the original E36xx7290A0 and a new 40011046 / 40001339 series. The new revision is compatible with KE-2050, KE-2060 and FX-1 but not with the earlier KE-2010 to 2040. Check the revision against your model before you fit.
What pickup rate and life can I expect?
The Southern Machinery decks quote a 99.99 percent pickup rate and a service life of more than 24 months. These are the manufacturer's own claims, not catalogue figures, and real life depends on duty cycle, part abrasion and cleaning frequency; treat them as targets and confirm on your part.
Which parts need a gripper or slot nozzle instead of a vacuum tip?
Leaded and connector parts suit slot nozzles; bulky or polarised parts suit gripper nozzles across a 0.8 to 5.2 mm gripping range; large bodies, sockets and shields suit pipe nozzles with rubber tips. The catalogue lists these families for both the 700 and 2000 machine groups.
How do I order, and what is the lead time?
Send the nozzle type or the component drawing, the head model and the quantity. The Southern Machinery decks quote a one-week lead time on standard types, with sea freight and customs-clearance delivery offered. Prices are on enquiry; this page is not a quotation.
